narrative: Fire ecology work this week reframes disturbance as a heterogeneity-builder rather than a pure threat: prescribed burns in the Cerrado diversified plant-bee interaction networks, while a simulation study in temperate forests shows how failed regeneration and flammable invaders can lock landscapes into self-reinforcing fire traps. Climate and range papers lean toward refugia and vulnerability mapping, from the historical biogeography of Amolops torrent frogs to projected habitat loss for Alpine ibex under warming scenarios. Behavioural findings continue to push beyond thermoregulation as the default lens, with free-ranging lizards shown to actively regulate ultraviolet exposure and individual boldness structuring spatial interactions within a rodent community. A long-term simulation of an Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphin population highlights how tourist food-provisioning compounds other stressors to accelerate decline, though interventions targeting calf survival can reverse projected losses. On the invasion front, a meltdown between a naturalised tree and an introduced resin bee, alongside allelopathic and litter-legacy mechanisms, illustrates how one introduced species can pave the way for others. In conservation planning, a EU-wide screening exercise finds up to 10% of land could qualify as other-effective-area-based conservation measures, while a 30-year parrot monitoring dataset shows demographic rates keep shifting well past apparent recovery. Methods contributions cluster heavily around bioacoustic and eDNA tools for wildlife monitoring, including a new evolutionary algorithm for lighter-weight passive acoustic classifiers, and a biogeography rebuttal challenges a recent niche-shift claim for invasive grey squirrels, underscoring how sensitive such conclusions are to methodological choices.
